extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century readers of The Spectator; general educated public interested in manners, morality, and conduct
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting prescriptive criteria and behavioural guidelines embedded in early-18th-century Spectator essays about dreams, temper, benevolence, and the soul's happiness. The page is a series of short moral and social essays (Addison, Grove, Budgell) addressing proper conduct and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of noisy morning criers as remembrancers
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of suppressing this Order of Mortals, make the best Advantage of their Morning Salutations; regard him as a kind of Remembrancer, come to admonish him that it is time to return to the Circumstances he has overlooked all the Night-time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay gives many examples where noisy early-risers both cause mischief (disturbing kings, interrupting fortunes) and avert misfortunes (waking a man who thereby avoided prison, a watchman who saved a man from enemies). Practical guidance: do not seek to silence them wholesale; treat them as helpful reminders to leave fanciful imaginations and attend to real duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disregard imaginary adventures occurring during sleep
rubrics_metrics.description: People may dream on as long as they please, but I shall take no Notice of any Imaginary Adventures that do not happen while the Sun is on this Side of the Horizon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts a rule for reporting or attending to 'adventures': only those experienced while awake (i.e., with the sun up) merit notice. Example: the author stifles Fritilla's church-dream about losing money and pawning children as not worth attention because it occurred in sleep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation between Merry and Serious temperaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Mankind may be divided into the Merry and the Serious... both make a very good Figure in the Species, so long as they keep their respective Humours from degenerating into the neighbouring Extreme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each temperament has virtues if kept from excess; the criterion is avoidance of extremes. The essay details the natural tendencies (merry→levity→folly; serious→moroseness) and recommends balance as the ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate timing and occasion for cheerfulness
rubrics_metrics.description: The merry Part of the World are very amiable, whilst they diffuse a Chearfulness through Conversation at proper Seasons and on proper Occasions; but... a great Grievance to Society, when they infect every Discourse with insipid Mirth, and turn into Ridicule such Subjects as are not suited to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter and mirth are valuable when applied suitably; excess or inappropriate levity marks folly. The philosophical note: laughter is a property of reason, but must be temperate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seriousness must be cheerful and humane
rubrics_metrics.description: Seriousness has its Beauty whilst it is attended with Chearfulness and Humanity, and does not come in unseasonably to pall the good Humour of those with whom we converse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seriousness is praised provided it retains warmth and humanity; unseasonable austerity that spoils others' good humour is condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal character blends humour and gravity
rubrics_metrics.description: The most perfect Character is that which is formed out of both of them... A Man would neither chuse to be a Hermit nor a Buffoon: Humane Nature is not so miserable, as that we should be always melancholy; nor so happy, as that we should be always merry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation: cultivate a temper that draws on both merry and serious qualities. The author argues that the perfect comportment uses the advantages of both temperaments without succumbing to either extreme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levity exposes one to temptation and vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Levity of Tamper takes a Man off his Guard, and opens a Pass to his Soul for any Temptation that assaults it. It favours all the Approaches of Vice, and weakens all the Resistance of Virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: take seriousness as a guard against moral danger; historical anecdote: a statesman advised friends 'Be serious' after retiring to religion, implying seriousness as moral protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-observation or disciplined withdrawal to correct imagination (Trophonius's Cave)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuing the Imagination through all its Extravagancies, whether in Sleeping or Waking, is no improper Method of correcting and bringing it to act in Subordinancy to Reason... the Cave of Trophonius would contribute more to the Reformation of Manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The allegory of admitting people to a solemn cave that enforces seriousness is used as a model: disciplinary retreat or systematic self-observation can reform excessive levity and bring imagination under reason. Examples: actors, coquettes, and others emerge more composed after the 'experiment.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish benevolence by obstinate persistence in good acts
rubrics_metrics.description: A great deal may be done by a Course of Beneficence obstinately persisted in; this, if any thing, being a likely way of establishing a moral Habit, which shall be somewhat of a Counterpoise to the Force of Mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where natural disposition resists beneficence (bodily temperament or ingrained character), persistent practice of good acts is the recommended method to form moral habits. Note: such habits require continuous reinforcement or they will lapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive love of the world; virtue increases by sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Worldly Things are of such a Quality as to lessen upon dividing... Virtue is a Good of a nobler kind; it grows by Communication, and so little resembles earthly Riches, that the more Hands it is lodged in, the greater is every Man's particular Stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical counsel: desire only what is necessary, view worldly goods as limited (fostering rivalry), and cultivate virtue through sharing and communication, which amplifies rather than diminishes happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain mental ease and contentment to enable benevolence
rubrics_metrics.description: Uneasiness of any Kind... hath not Leisure to attend to the Necessity or Reasonableness of a Kindness desired... The most miserable of all Beings is the most envious; as, on the other hand, the most communicative is the happiest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be generous, one needs a calm, satisfied mind. Advice includes choosing the softest times to request favors and cultivating confidence in providence and self-satisfaction to promote good-will toward others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of pleasures composes the soul's happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The Soul consists of many Faculties... every Faculty is as a distinct Taste in the Mind, and hath Objects accommodated to its proper Relish... there is an infinite Variety in those Pleasures we are speaking of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argumentative standard for what constitutes perfect happiness (in an afterlife): happiness will include varied satisfactions addressing different faculties (understanding, memory, will, imagination, senses). Revelation and reason both support this multiplicity of pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creator would not make unused faculties; happiness should employ all faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: There cannot be a stronger Argument that God has designed us for a State of future Happiness... he has thus naturally qualified the Soul for it, and made it a Being capable of receiving so much Bliss. He would never have made such Faculties in vain...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evaluative criterion: any theory of future happiness should account for the multiple faculties of the soul; the existence of faculties implies they are meant to be exercised and rewarded. Used as moral encouragement to cultivate faculties now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculties relieve one another and gain from novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The Faculties relieve one another by Turns, and receive an additional Pleasure from the Novelty of those Objects about which they are conversant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing personal happiness or designing a good life, include alternation of activities and novelty to keep faculties refreshed; this supports the argument for variety in felicity.
